questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Quoting the person you disagree with
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a quotation fair to the speaker
questions.stem: A rebuttal quotes a field note in a way that changes its meaning. Explain what makes a quotation a fair representation of the person being disagreed with.

answer.exemplar: A fair quotation reproduces the speaker's words without stitching in or dropping wording, and it is given in the context the speaker gave it. If the quoted words would let a reader who had not been there reach the opposite conclusion, the quotation has been trimmed to make the case rather than to report the position.

questions.explanation: A quotation is fair when the words, the emphasis and the context are the speaker's own, so a reader would recognise the position. Trimming or stitching changes the claim being argued with.
questions.hint: Ask whether the speaker would recognise the position.

questions.topic: Synthesis that changes both positions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a synthesis changes both positions
questions.stem: Describe what a synthesis must do to both positions in a survey dispute if it is to change the argument rather than summarise it.

answer.exemplar: A synthesis that changes both positions states the shared premise the two sides have not contested, shows how each side's reading of the data follows from that premise, and names what would have to be true for both readings to be defensible. answer.exemplar: The disputed reading would have been settled by a photograph or a field sketch made on the day, since either would have recorded the state of the bank before the channel was dug. questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Quoting the person you disagree with
questions.learningObjective: Explain how quoting can misrepresent
questions.stem: Explain how quoting a colleague's words can be used to misrepresent them, and what a careful quotation does instead.

answer.exemplar: Words can be misrepresented by trimming a sentence, by joining two remarks that were made apart, by keeping a qualification that was tentative and dropping the reason for the doubt, or by choosing punctuation that reverses the sense. A careful quotation keeps the speaker's words in their original order, keeps the qualifications attached, and says where the words came from.

questions.explanation: Misquoting works by changing context, order or emphasis while leaving the words technically intact, so the reader is misled about the position.
questions.hint: Ask what the speaker said immediately before and after.

questions.topic: Concessions that cost more than they gain
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a concession earns its cost
questions.stem: Which concession in this dispute would be best used to keep the reviewer's support for the team's findings?

options.text: The team concedes the narrow point it can defend and holds firm on the one that carries the argument.
The team concedes the point that carries the argument, since it is the harder one to defend.
options.misconception: concedes the load-bearing claim to avoid defending it

options.text: The team concedes everything the reviewer asks for, which ends the disagreement quickly.
options.misconception: buys peace at the cost of the whole finding

options.text: The team concedes nothing, since a concession would show the team was unsure of its own data.
options.misconception: treats a concession as evidence of weakness in the team

questions.explanation: A trades away what it can defend and protects what carries the finding, keeping the reviewer's support. B concedes the load-bearing claim, C buys peace at the cost of the result, and D will not move.
questions.hint: Ask which point the rest of the finding depends on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Synthesis that changes both positions
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a synthesis changes both positions
questions.stem: Explain how a synthesis can change both positions in a survey dispute, and what makes that change durable.

answer.exemplar: A synthesis changes both positions by identifying the premise the two sides already share and then showing each side what it must now defend on that premise, which is often less than it thought. The change is durable when it is written into the next piece of work, so that each party's next action is governed by the shared framing rather than by the old disagreement, and when neither side can simply revert to its former claim without explaining itself.

questions.explanation: Synthesis changes positions by re-framing what each side must defend, and the change lasts when the next work is built on that framing.
questions.hint: Ask what each side must now defend instead.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A standard of proof changed mid-argument
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a shift in the standard of proof

stimulus.body: Team: The claim that the scheme reduced sediment in the pool needs the pool sediment depth to have been measured before the works. Reviewer: Then the claim cannot be made. Team: We agree the claim cannot be made on that basis, but it may still be supported by the trapped sediment in the outfall.

questions.stem: Which reading best captures what the team's last sentence does?

options.text: It raises the standard of proof by adding a second condition that must also be met.
options.misconception: reads an alternative line of support as a raised bar

options.text: It lowers the standard of proof by offering a different kind of evidence for the same claim.
It withdraws the claim outright, since the team says the original basis does not hold.
options.misconception: misses that the claim is being rebuilt rather than dropped

options.text: It changes the topic, moving the dispute from sediment to the behaviour of the outfall.
options.misconception: treats a supporting route as a change of subject

questions.explanation: The claim stands or falls on evidence, and the team offers a different route to the same conclusion, so the standard has not moved. A and C misread the move, and D calls it a change of subject.
questions.hint: Ask what the team is offering instead of what it gives up.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What evidence would have been worth having
questions.learningObjective: Specify the evidence that would have settled the dispute
questions.stem: Which reply identifies the evidence that would now settle the survey dispute most directly?

options.text: The full record of the eleven comparison wells, since the report simply omitted them.
options.misconception: assumes the omitted records exist and would help the team

options.text: A statement from the client confirming that the survey was commissioned as described.
options.misconception: proposes a record of the commission rather than of the site

options.text: Sediment depth at the pool measured before and after the works, since that is what is missing.
A second opinion from a hydrologist who has worked on comparable schemes elsewhere.
options.misconception: answers an evidential question with another opinion

questions.explanation: The dispute turns on a before-and-after sediment measurement that was never made, and C names it. A assumes records that may not exist, B concerns the commission, and D is an opinion.
questions.hint: Ask what measurement would show the claim to hold.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Concessions that cost more than they gain
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a concession earns its cost
questions.stem: First determine whether conceding protects the team's own findings or weakens them, then choose the reply.

options.text: It weakens them, so the team should withdraw the concession and restore the original wording.
options.misconception: restores a wording that was conceded for a reason

options.text: It protects them, so the team should make the concession public as a show of good faith.
options.misconception: publishes a concession for the sake of appearance

options.text: It weakens them, so the team should ask the reviewer to state the concession in writing.
options.misconception: seeks paperwork instead of dealing with the substance

options.text: It protects them, because the concession removes a point the reviewer was using.

questions.explanation: A concession protects the team's findings when it withdraws a point the other side was deploying against them, which D identifies. A and C respond to the wrong problem, and B seeks appearances.
questions.hint: Ask what the reviewer was doing with the point.
